en: The Sūtra on the Eight Unfavourable Conditions and the Favourable Condition Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jetavana Grove.
At the Jetavana Grove, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, as well as gods and humans.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"You should know that in this world, there are those who are of little learning and lacking in knowledge—ordinary persons—who constantly speak of 'opportunities' and 'non-opportunities,' yet they do not understand what constitutes a non-opportunity and what constitutes an opportunity."
I shall now analyze and explain this for you; listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
"If there are sentient beings who wish to abide in noble conduct and cultivate wholesome dharmas, there are eight circumstances in which they lack the leisure to practice."
What are the eight? You should know this:

"In this world, a Great Teacher has appeared—namely, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—who proclaims the sublime Dharma realized by all Buddhas, which skillfully removes afflictions, leads toward Bodhi, culminates in Nirvāṇa, and brings an end to all suffering."

When this Dharma was being taught, there were some who had fallen into the hells and were undergoing great suffering; this is called the first instance of being without leisure to practice while desiring to abide in noble conduct.

"Furthermore, monks! In this world, a Great Teacher appears, endowed with the ten titles, who proclaims the sublime Dharma realized by all Buddhas—a Dharma that effectively removes the afflictions, leads to enlightenment, culminates in final nirvana, and brings an end to all suffering."

When this Dharma was being taught, there were those who had fallen among the hungry ghosts and were undergoing great suffering; this is called the second occasion of non-leisure for one who wishes to abide in noble conduct but lacks the opportunity for cultivation.

"Furthermore, monks! In this world, a Great Teacher appears, endowed with the ten titles, who proclaims the sublime Dharma realized by all Buddhas—a Dharma that skillfully removes afflictions, leads to enlightenment, results in ultimate nirvana, and brings an end to all suffering."

When this Dharma was being taught, there were those who had fallen among the animals and were undergoing various sufferings; this is called the third lack of leisure for practicing the noble conduct while desiring to abide in it.

"Furthermore, monks! In this world, a Great Teacher appears, endowed with the ten titles, proclaiming the sublime Dharma realized by all Buddhas—a Dharma that skillfully removes afflictions, leads to enlightenment, culminates in ultimate nirvana, and brings an end to all suffering."

When this Dharma was being taught, there were those born in the Heaven of Long Life who lacked understanding; this is called the fourth occasion of non-leisure for one wishing to abide in noble conduct and practice cultivation.

"Furthermore, monks! In this world, a Great Teacher appears, endowed with the ten titles, proclaiming the sublime Dharma realized by all Buddhas—a teaching that effectively removes the afflictions, leads toward enlightenment, culminates in final nirvana, and brings an end to all suffering."

When this Dharma was being taught, there were those born in remote borderlands, among the lowly, or among the Mlecchas, who did not recognize good from evil and neither heard nor saw my fourfold assembly; this is called the fifth lack of leisure for practicing the noble conduct while desiring to abide therein.

"Furthermore, monks! In this world, a Great Teacher appears, endowed with the ten titles, proclaiming the sublime Dharma realized by all Buddhas—a Dharma that skillfully removes afflictions, leads toward enlightenment, culminates in ultimate nirvana, and brings an end to all suffering."

When this Dharma was being taught, there were those who, although born in the Central Land, nevertheless received evil retribution—being deaf, blind, or mute—and communicating by means of hand gestures, unable to distinguish between good and evil. This is called the sixth lack of leisure for practicing the noble conduct while desiring to abide in it.
"Furthermore, O bhikṣus!

In this world, a Great Teacher appears, endowed with the ten titles, proclaiming the sublime Dharma realized by all Buddhas—a Dharma that skillfully removes the afflictions, leads to enlightenment, culminates in ultimate nirvāṇa, and brings an end to all suffering."

When this Dharma was being taught, there were some who, though born in the Central Land and whose bodies were neither deaf, blind, nor mute—nor did they need to speak through gestures—and who were fully capable of discerning between good and evil, nevertheless believed in heterodox views and held such opinions as these:

"There is no giving and no receiving, nor is there any sacrificial offering; there are no causes and conditions for good or evil karma, nor is there any ripening of karmic fruit; there is no present life or future life, no parents or kin, and no sentient beings born by transformation."

In this world, there are no arhats who have rightly entered the path and rightly practiced, who, in this very life and in the world beyond, have attained self-awakening, realized perfection, and fully understood: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there will be no further existence."
"All these things do not exist.
Thus he gives rise to extreme wrong views; this is called the seventh occasion of non-leisure for one who wishes to abide in noble conduct and practice its cultivation. Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!

In this world, no Great Teacher has appeared; there is no one bearing the Ten Epithets; the sublime Dharma realized by the Buddhas is not heard; afflictions are not eliminated; one does not proceed toward Bodhi, nor reach Nirvana, and there is no end to suffering.

There may be someone who, though born in the central land, is neither deaf, blind, nor mute, and does not communicate by means of hand gestures; who understands both good and evil, does not give rise to false views, and speaks thus:

"There is giving and there is receiving; there are also sacrificial offerings; there are causes and conditions consisting of good and evil karma; there are the ripening fruits of retribution; there are this world and future worlds; there are parents and kinsmen; and there are sentient beings born by transformation."

In this world, there are Arhats who have entered the right path and practice rightly; having attained self-awakening and realized perfect fulfillment within this very life regarding both this world and the next, they fully understand: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there will be no further existence."
"All these exist," he thinks,
and thus gives rise to perfect right view; yet,
there is no guide to open the door of liberation— this is called the eighth state of being without leisure for practicing the noble conduct because one wishes to abide therein.

"Furthermore, monks! In this world, a Great Teacher appears, endowed with the ten titles, proclaiming the sublime Dharma realized by all Buddhas—a Dharma that skillfully removes afflictions, leads to enlightenment, results in ultimate nirvana, and brings an end to all suffering."

When this Dharma was being taught, there were those born in the central land whose physical bodies possessed all faculties intact, who understood the words of both good and evil, and even gave rise to the most correct view.
"O bhikṣus, you should know that this person possesses the leisure for practice. O bhikṣus, you have already obtained these conditions of leisure:

being born in a central land, encountering my appearance in the world, hearing the holy teaching, and having all faculties complete. You should give rise to valor and always exert yourselves with diligence to cultivate all wholesome qualities. Within the sublime Dharma and Vinaya, practice according to the instructions, teach one another in turn, and repent of one another’s faults. Always purify the three karmas and constantly practice the ten wholesome paths; do not engage in what is useless so as to bring about future regret."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I have already explained the eight states of no-leisure; I pray that you all shall be born within the state of leisure.
If one is born in a place of difficulty and does not hear this sutra, You should listen with a sincere and focused mind."
Pressed by manifold sufferings of copper pillars and iron mountains, Of glowing embers, excrement, and forests of sword-blades—
Enduring such torments within the hells, How could one hear the True Dharma in such a place?
Starving and parched, the agony of needles piercing their throats oppresses their bodies; where rain falls like rivers, it becomes fierce fire.
Suffering such torments among the hungry ghosts (preta), how could they ever hear the True Dharma here?
Constantly harboring hearts of fear and malice toward one another, they always desire to devour each other in turn;
undergoing such suffering among the animals, how could they ever hear the True Dharma in this place?

If one is among the gods in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), having been born there by the power of prior merit, one’s lifespan is long and one’s awakening-wisdom is indistinct; how could the True Dharma be heard in such a place?
Born in a remote and despicable region, never having heard the sound of the Dharma being preached,
ignorant and always dwelling among the Mlecchas— how could one hear the True Dharma in such a place?
Due to the evil karma created in previous lives, they are deaf, blind, mute, and deficient in their faculties;
being dull-witted and stupid, such people are like oxen among humans—how could they ever hear the True Dharma?
If a person does not have faith in the Triple Gem, And asserts that there is no cause and effect and no honored kin,
With such wrong views destroying their mind, How could this person ever hear the True Dharma?
When the Great Teachers, the Buddhas, do not appear, And the sublime Dharma does not flow through the world,
If a person dwells within this age of darkness, How could they hear the True Dharma at such a time?
If one is born in a state of leisure, with all eight kinds of obstacles to leisure removed,
like a patient who has encountered a skilled physician, one should listen to the True Dharma with a sincere heart!
Having already obtained a human body and further having heard the True Dharma, if one does not attain the fruits of holiness, one will be born many times in states lacking leisure.
I have spoken of the eight states of no leisure; these are difficult places for sentient beings.
To have attained a life of leisure is rare indeed among the people of this world.
Having already obtained a human body and further having heard the True Dharma,
those who cherish themselves should eliminate their afflictions and pride.
If one hears the True Dharma but cannot practice according to what was taught,
they will wander through the eight states of adversity, undergoing all manner of suffering.
Having already abandoned these states of no leisure, one should constantly seek to hear the True Dharma.
Amidst birth, old age, and death, one shall soon attain liberation.
Having already obtained a human body, if one hears the Dharma yet acts with negligence,
one will later give rise to distress and regret, like a merchant who has lost his wealth.
If a person hears my teaching on the states of leisure and non-leisure,
they should therefore apply themselves with a diligent mind to the correct cultivation of the holy life.
I declare that such a person is one with clear vision, who well guards against all evils.
Right mindfulness can guard [the mind], so that one does not follow after the outflows (*āsrava*).
With all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) severed, one subdues the great enemy, Māra;
forever transcending the stream of birth and death, one attains the crossing to the other shore.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the assembly of bhikṣus, devas, humans, and the great multitude, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced, received it upon their heads with reverence, and faithfully practiced it.
The Sūtra on the Eight States of No Leisure and the State of Leisure Spoken by the Buddha.
